title: The cost of fear: prior predator-cue experience and current cue intensity modify habitat selection and reproduction in a spider mite
content:
Abstract
Predation suppresses prey populations not only through direct consumption but also through non-consumptive effects that alter behavior, reproduction, and population dynamics. However, how prior exposure to predator cues influences these responses across heterogeneous environments differing in predator-cue intensity remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of predator cues derived from the predatory mite Phytoseiulus persimilis on habitat selection, reproduction, offspring performance, adult emergence trajectories, and population growth of the spider mite Tetranychus ludeni. T. ludeni females with or without prior predator-cue experience were exposed to habitats differing in predator tracks and predator egg density. Non-experienced females strongly avoided habitats with high predator-cue intensities, whereas experienced females reduced discrimination among risky levels, indicating altered predator-cue assessment following early-life exposure. Predator cues significantly reduced fecundity, egg hatching, and population growth, with stronger suppression generally occurring in experienced females. Predator-associated habitats also increased the daughter proportion, although experienced females produced fewer daughters overall, particularly under predator-free conditions, suggesting stress-mediated shifts in sex allocation. Increasing predator-cue intensity reduced the asymptotic emergence of daughters, which directly contributed to lower intrinsic (rm) and finite rates of increase (λ) and a longer doubling time (Dt). However, the timing of offspring emergence remained largely unchanged, indicating that predator cues primarily suppressed recruitment magnitude rather than developmental rate. Our findings demonstrate that predator cues alone can substantially suppress prey populations through integrated behavioral, reproductive, developmental, and transgenerational pathways. These results highlight the ecological importance of non-consumptive predation effects and suggest that predator-induced cues may enhance long-term pest suppression in biological control programs.
